title: SYSK Selects: How a Flea Circus Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on flea circuses, chosen by Josh as one of his all-time favorites. The hosts trace flea circuses from Mark Scalliot, a 1570s London blacksmith who used a flea as a prop, to Louis Bertelotto, the 1820s Italian impresario who made fleas the stars of his show. They cover why fleas were used (ubiquity, jumping ability and elastic cuticle energy storage), the acts (chariot pulling, sword fighting, soccer, juggling, high wire, Napoleon at Waterloo, dressed Mexican-made flea costumes), and the harnessing and gluing methods used on the fleas. They discuss William Heckler and his son's American flea circuses in the early twentieth century, the feeding of fleas on the performer's blood, and the decline of the trade. The episode also covers humbug (fake) flea circuses using magnets and mechanical devices, Michael Bentine's 1950 Royal Variety Show act, Tom Palmer's booklet on humbug flea acts, Maria Fernanda Cardoso's 1990s performance art flea circus, and animal-welfare objections. The episode ends with a listener mail from a teacher, Sarah Amato, about using the show in her classes.

segments.title: Selects intro and flea circus overview
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as one of his favorites from the archive. The hosts say flea circuses were covered briefly before, and note how little documentation exists and how much misinformation is out there.

segments.title: Early flea showmen and why fleas
segments.summary: The hosts describe Mark Scalliot, a London blacksmith in the 1570s who used a flea as a prop to show off tiny work. They explain why fleas were chosen: they were ubiquitous and could jump far, aided by elastic cuticles storing energy. A Royal Air Force Experimental Station study of jumping is mentioned.

segments.title: Louis Bertelotto and early flea acts
segments.summary: Louis Bertelotto, an 1820s Italian impresario in London, made fleas the stars of his show. Acts included chariot pulling, high wire, sword fighting, historical reenactments such as Waterloo, soccer, and high diving. Touring and keeping fleas alive was difficult, and Bertelotto later reportedly vanished into anonymity in Canada.

segments.title: Heckler and American flea circuses
segments.summary: William Heckler became a successful American flea master in the early 1900s, performing at fairs and carnivals with many shows a day. The hosts describe the logistics of rapid audience turnover and the work involved in keeping fleas alive, with fleas shipped from Majorca.

segments.title: How the fleas were harnessed and staged
segments.summary: The hosts explain the harness of silk thread or fine gold wire, the selection of fleas, the jar-lid and sticky-foothold legends attributed to Heckler, and the gluing of props to fleas. Staged acts such as sword fighting, soccer using citronella-soaked cotton, juggling, and heat-driven dancing are described.

segments.title: Flea costumes and feeding on blood
segments.summary: The hosts describe flea costumes made by Mexican nuns, displayed today at the Rothschild Zoological Museum in England and a museum in Edinburgh. They describe how performers fed fleas on their own blood, sometimes at the end of shows.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: A short break in the episode.

segments.title: Humbug flea circuses and Michael Bentine
segments.summary: The hosts explain humbug flea circuses that use no real fleas and rely on illusion, magnets and mechanical devices. George Tollerton wrote about fake acts, and Michael Bentine performed an elaborate fake act at the 1950 Royal Variety Show. Tom Palmer's booklet The Famous Flea Act is mentioned.

segments.title: Modern flea circuses and animal welfare
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Maria Fernanda Cardoso's 1990s performance-art flea circus with live fleas, shown in New York and San Francisco. They mention animal-welfare groups calling for flea circuses to be banned, and note the continuing German flea circus at Munich Oktoberfest.

segments.title: Listener mail from teacher Sarah Amato
segments.summary: A listener writes that the show is used in her high school and community college English classes, including episodes on book banning, police interrogation, and hunting arguments. Josh and Chuck thank her and read out social media and contact information.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode with the usual sign-off and contact details.
